content: 1. Do not abruptly stop taking atenolol without consulting your doctor. Stopping atenolol suddenly can lead to serious complications such as chest pain, heart attack, or irregular heartbeat. Your doctor will likely reduce your dose gradually to prevent these issues. 2. Atenolol is prescribed to manage high blood pressure, either alone or in combination with other medications. It is also used to prevent angina (chest pain) and to treat heart attacks. Atenolol belongs to a class of drugs called beta blockers, which work by slowing the heart rate and relaxing blood vessels, reducing the workload on the heart. 3. Atenolol is available as an oral tablet and is typically taken once or twice daily. To ensure consistency, take it at the same time each day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take atenolol exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency unless advised by your doctor. 4. Atenolol helps control high blood pressure and angina but does not cure these conditions. It may take 1-2 weeks to experience the full benefits of the medication. Continue taking atenolol even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. 5. Atenolol is sometimes used for other purposes, such as preventing migraine headaches, managing alcohol withdrawal, treating heart failure, and addressing irregular heartbeats. Discuss the potential risks and benefits of using atenolol for these conditions with your doctor. 6. Before taking atenolol, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to atenolol or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. This includes calcium channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem, verapamil), clonidine, NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin), and reserpine, as these may interact with atenolol. 7. Notify your doctor if you have a history of asthma, lung disease, diabetes, severe allergies, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, heart failure, slow heart rate, circulation problems, or heart or kidney disease. 8. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking atenolol, contact your doctor immediately. 9. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking atenolol. Be aware that atenolol may worsen allergic reactions and reduce the effectiveness of injectable epinephrine in treating severe allergic reactions. 10. If your doctor prescribes a low-salt or low-sodium diet, follow these dietary instructions carefully. 11. If you miss a dose of atenolol, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. 12. Atenolol may cause side effects. Common minor side effects include dizziness, lightheadedness, tiredness, drowsiness, depression, upset stomach, and diarrhea. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. 13. Serious side effects, though uncommon, require immediate medical attention. These include shortness of breath, swelling of the hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, unusual weight gain, and fainting. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. 14. Atenolol may cause other side effects. Report any unusual problems to your doctor. Serious side effects can also be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. 15. Store atenolol in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. 16. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include fatigue, difficulty breathing, wheezing, slow heartbeat, fainting, swelling of the extremities, unusual weight gain, shakiness, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, sweating, confusion, blurred vision, headache, numbness or tingling in the mouth, weakness, excessive tiredness, pale skin, or sudden hunger. 17. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Regular monitoring of your blood pressure and heart rate is essential to assess your response to atenolol. Your doctor may ask you to check your pulse regularly. If your pulse is abnormally fast or slow, contact your doctor. 18. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist or doctor if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
